titulo: Terrain curriculum and your training plan
lead: Nobody trains stair walking on day one: the terrain and the requested speed grow as the policy succeeds. In this lesson you measure how far up the ladder the ready-made policy goes, read how mjlab and unitree_rl_lab level up, and write your own training plan in a file that a script checks.
objetivo: measure the ready-made policy's maximum step, read the curriculum rules, and write a training plan with 5 fields that conferir_plano.py approves.

aprende.t: Steps of 2 and 3 cm pass; from 4 cm up, it falls
Curriculum: it moves up if it walked more than 80% of the request, down if it walked less than 50%
Command curriculum: the speed range opens 0.1 m/s at a time
The plano-treino.md with robot, command, reward, curriculum and evaluation

hero_alt: Test track in a dark lab with a wooden ramp, low steps and pebbles, and a humanoid robot climbing the first step attached to a safety rail.

secoes.sub: Click each level. Each robot moves up or down a level on its own, based on how far it walked.

nos.detalhe: Every training run starts on flat ground. The terrain generator in unitree_rl_lab (commit 4960b84) has a single sub-terrain, flat: the ready-made policy was trained on flat ground only.
Steps a few centimeters high. The ready-made policy, trained only on flat ground, clears 2 and 3 cm in the kit's test and falls from 4 cm on.
Ramps require the policy to adjust its stride to the slope. Next level of a typical curriculum.

Uneven terrain (pebbles, blocks). The next level only opens for those who passed the previous one: in mjlab, you move up if you walked more than 80% of the requested distance, and you move down if you walked less than 50%.

secoes.legenda: Rules read from the code: mjlab mdp/curriculums.py (commit 8bb2bc9) and unitree_rl_lab velocity_env_cfg.py (commit 4960b84).

secoes.titulo: How far up the steps the ready-made policy goes
secoes.sub: terreno.py uses MjSpec to build a platform of height h 1.5 m from the robot and tells it to walk for 8 s at 0.5 m/s. Passed = it did not fall and the pelvis ended up on top (x > 2.5 m).

2 and 3 cm pass; from 4 cm up, the robot falls at x ≈ 2 m, before getting onto the platform. The steps that fail are the next levels of a curriculum: that is what you retrain for.

secoes.titulo: How the repositories move up a level
secoes.sub: Two curricula run together in real training. Click each one.

texto: In mjlab, at the end of each episode, a robot that walked more than 80% of the requested distance moves up one terrain level; one that walked less than 50% moves down. Each robot has its own level: in the same training run, some are on flat ground and others on pebbles.
In unitree_rl_lab, the requested velocity starts at ±0.1 m/s. When velocity tracking passes 80% of the maximum, the range opens 0.1 m/s on each side, up to the limit of −0.5 to 1.0 m/s.

The push is not part of the curriculum in these two repositories: ±0.5 m/s in x and y, every 5 s in unitree_rl_lab; in mjlab, every 1 to 3 s, with ±0.4 m/s in z as well and roll, pitch, and yaw rotations.
Before spending GPU: which robot, what command range, which terms and weights, what terrain levels, and which test approves. It is the file you write now.

secoes.sub: Copy the template to ~/fth/treino, replace each [bracket] with your value, and check it. The kit example shows a plan that passes.

blocos.conteudo:
# Plano de treino de locomoção

Robô: [qual humanoide e qual arquivo, ex.: Unitree G1 29 GDL, unitree_g1/scene.xml do Menagerie 62ab00f]
Comando: [faixa de velocidade, ex.: vx de -0.5 a 1.0 m/s, vy de -0.3 a 0.3 m/s, giro de -0.2 a 0.2 rad/s]
Recompensa: [termos e pesos, ex.: track_linear_velocity 2.0, upright 1.0, action_rate_l2 -0.1]
Currículo: [níveis em ordem, separados por →, ex.: plano → degrau de 5 cm → rampa → pedriscos]
Avaliação: [critério de aprovação com número, ex.: 18/20 episódios de pé com empurrão de 1.0 m/s]

F=${FTH:-$HOME/fth}; cd $F/locomocao && . $F/.venv/bin/activate
[ -f $F/treino/plano-treino.md ] || cp kit/plano-treino-modelo.md $F/treino/plano-treino.md
python3 kit/conferir_plano.py $F/treino/plano-treino.md; echo "saída: $?"

F=${FTH:-$HOME/fth}; cd $F/locomocao && . $F/.venv/bin/activate
python3 kit/conferir_plano.py kit/exemplos/plano-treino.md; echo "saída: $?"

With the template still full of [brackets], all five fields are missing and the script exits with 1. Rules: command with a number and m/s, reward with 2 or more kit terms, curriculum with 3 or more levels separated by →, evaluation with a numeric criterion (X/N or %).

campos ok: 5/5
ok
saída: 0

The kit example (kit/exemplos/plano-treino.md) uses the command ranges from unitree_rl_lab and the 18/20 criterion from lesson 7.

secoes.sub: The explanation appears after your answer.

perguntas.p: In mjlab's terrain curriculum, when does a robot move up a level?
opcoes: Every 1,000 training iterations, for all robots in the training run at the same time.
When the training's average reward goes above zero.
When the operator changes the level in the configuration file.
When, at the end of the episode, it walked more than 80 % of the requested distance.
perguntas.explica: The level is per robot and decided by what it did. A robot that walks less than 50 % of what was asked moves down: the curriculum adjusts itself.

perguntas.p: The finished policy clears 3 cm steps and falls at 4 cm. In a training plan, what do you do with that?
opcoes: Swap the robot for another one with longer legs.
Make the steps that failed the next levels of the curriculum.
Raise the ankle kp until the policy can climb the 4 cm without falling.
Take the steps out of the evaluation so the policy passes.
perguntas.explica: The terrain test shows where the policy stops; the curriculum is the way to get past that point. Changing the gains invalidates the policy (lesson 2).

perguntas.p: Why does unitree_rl_lab start by asking for only ±0.1 m/s?
opcoes: Because the G1 doesn't walk above 0.1 m/s at the start of the run.
Because Isaac Lab limits the robot's speed during the first thousand training iterations.
To learn the easy part first; the range opens when tracking passes 80 %.
Because higher speeds call for a different robot in training.
perguntas.explica: It's a command curriculum: it starts where the policy can get it right and opens 0.1 m/s at a time up to −0.5 to 1.0 m/s.

itens.texto: The finished policy clears 2 cm and 3 cm steps and falls from 4 cm on.
Terrain moves up at 80 % of the distance and down below 50 %; the command opens 0.1 m/s at a time.
Robot, command, reward, curriculum, and evaluation written and checked before training.
